t: Under the Insurance Act, 1938, the power to make rules rests with the Central Government under Section 114, while the power to make regulations rests with:
o: the Life Insurance Council
IRDAI under Section 114A
the Reserve Bank of India
the Insurance Advisory Committee
e: Rules and regulations are both forms of delegated legislation; regulations under S.114A are framed by the Authority, laid before Parliament, and cover matters such as policyholder protection, products and intermediaries.

t: Under Article 13 of the Constitution, a law that is inconsistent with the fundamental rights is:
o: valid if passed by a two-thirds majority
valid until Parliament repeals it
void to the extent of the inconsistency
void only if the President withholds assent
e: Article 13 makes the Constitution the supreme source of law; pre- and post-Constitution laws inconsistent with Part III are void to that extent, and courts may strike them down.

t: The Indian Penal Code, 1860 has been replaced with effect from 1 July 2024 by the:
o: Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023
e: The three new criminal laws replaced the IPC, CrPC and Evidence Act respectively; insurance fraud and forgery of claim documents are now punishable under the BNS.

t: In a suit by a nominee on a repudiated life policy, the burden of proving that the life assured suppressed a material fact lies on:
o: the insurer, which asserts the suppression
the nominee, as the plaintiff
the agent who canvassed the policy
IRDAI
e: He who asserts must prove: the insurer pleading non-disclosure or fraud must establish it with evidence, a position reinforced by Section 45(2) which requires the insurer to communicate its materials.

t: Under Section 22 of the Indian Contract Act, a contract is NOT voidable merely because:
o: consent was caused by coercion
one party alone was under a mistake as to a matter of fact
both parties were under a mistake as to an essential fact
consent was caused by fraud
e: A unilateral mistake of fact does not affect the contract; only a bilateral mistake of essential fact (S.20) makes it void, while fraud and coercion make it voidable.

t: Under Section 4 of the Indian Contract Act, the communication of an acceptance is complete as against the proposer:
o: when the proposer acknowledges receipt
when it comes to the knowledge of the proposer
when it is put in a course of transmission to him so as to be out of the power of the acceptor
when the acceptor decides to accept
e: Once the letter of acceptance is posted, the proposer is bound; as against the acceptor it is complete only when it reaches the proposer, so the acceptor can revoke before that.

t: Under Section 2(d) of the Indian Contract Act, consideration must move:
o: at the desire of the promisor, from the promisee or any other person
only from the promisee
only in the form of money
before the promise is made
e: Indian law permits consideration to move from a third party (unlike English law), provided it is at the promisor's desire; it may be past, present or future.

t: Under Section 39 of the Insurance Act, 1938, a nomination can be made by:
o: an assignee of the policy
a creditor who has advanced a loan against the policy
the holder of a policy on his own life
any proposer, even on the life of another
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). Only the holder of a policy of life insurance on his own life may nominate; a nomination does not transfer any interest and is merely an authority to receive the money on death.

t: In life insurance underwriting, 'moral hazard' refers to:
o: the risk arising from the character, habits or intentions of the proposer, such as taking cover with a view to profit from death
the risk arising from the proposer's medical history
the risk arising from the proposer's occupation
the risk arising from the insurer's investment losses
e: Moral hazard concerns the honesty and motives of the proposer rather than physical factors; insurers guard against it through insurable interest, financial underwriting and the agent's confidential report.

t: In life insurance practice, the risk on the life assured ordinarily commences from the:
o: date of the medical examination
date of receipt of the first premium after acceptance of the proposal, as shown in the first premium receipt
date of signing the proposal form
date the policy bond is dispatched
e: The insurer assumes risk only after acceptance and receipt of premium (S.64VB); the first premium receipt records the date of commencement of risk, which may be backdated within limits.

t: Which of the following events does NOT restart the three-year period under Section 45 of the Insurance Act?
o: Revival of a lapsed policy
Addition of a rider to the policy
Change of nomination under the policy
Issuance of the policy
e: Section 45 counts from the date of issuance, commencement of risk, revival or rider addition, whichever is later; a nomination or its change does not alter the contract or restart the period.

t: Where a policy that has been revived provides a suicide clause of 12 months, the exclusion period is reckoned from:
o: the original date of commencement only
the date of the last premium paid
the date of nomination
the date of revival as well as the original date of commencement
e: The suicide clause applies afresh for 12 months from the date of revival, since revival is a fresh acceptance of risk; death by suicide within that period attracts the limited benefit.

t: Four years after a policy was issued, the insurer obtains conclusive proof that the life assured had fraudulently suppressed a terminal illness at proposal. On a death claim now, the insurer:
o: must pay the claim, as no policy can be called in question on any ground after three years
can pay only the premiums paid
can repudiate after obtaining IRDAI approval
can repudiate, as fraud has no time limit
e: The 2015 amendment made the three-year limit absolute, even for fraud; the insurer's remedy is to detect such cases within three years.

t: A 16-year participating endowment policy with sum assured ₹4,00,000 lapsed after four annual premiums, with vested bonuses of ₹30,000. The total paid-up value payable at maturity is:
e: Paid-up sum assured = 4,00,000 × 4/16 = ₹1,00,000; the bonuses already vested (₹30,000) remain attached, giving ₹1,30,000, with no future bonuses.

topic: Group Life and Other Insurance Schemes
t: The Employees' Provident Funds and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952 applies to every establishment employing:
o: 50 or more persons
10 or more persons
20 or more persons
100 or more persons
e: The Act (and with it the EDLI scheme) applies to notified establishments with 20 or more employees, and continues to apply even if the number later falls below 20.

topic: Group Life and Other Insurance Schemes
t: Under IRDAI's guidelines on group insurance, which of the following is NOT permitted?
o: Covering employees of an employer under a master policy
Issuing certificates of insurance to members
Collection of premium by the master policyholder from members
Forming a group solely for the purpose of availing insurance
e: A group must have a commonality of purpose other than insurance (employer-employee, bank customers, members of an association); groups formed only to buy insurance are not recognised.

topic: Group Life and Other Insurance Schemes
t: An employee with last drawn wages of ₹30,000 per month resigns after 7 years and 2 months of continuous service. The gratuity payable under the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 is approximately:
e: Gratuity = 30,000 × 15/26 × 7 = ₹1,21,154 (rounded); two months beyond seven years is less than six months and is not rounded up to a full year.

t: Where a policyholder nominates a minor, Section 39 provides that he may:
o: not nominate a minor at all
appoint any person (an 'appointee') to receive the money on behalf of the minor during minority
nominate only through a court order
nominate the minor only up to ₹1 lakh
e: An appointee ensures that a valid discharge can be given if the policyholder dies while the nominee is a minor; without one, the insurer pays the minor's guardian.

t: Under Section 6 of the Married Women's Property Act, 1874, where no trustee is appointed for the policy, the policy money vests in:
o: the insurer
the husband's legal heirs
the Official Trustee of the State in which the insurer's office is situated
the Life Insurance Council
e: The Act provides that in the absence of a named trustee, a trustee appointed by the court or the Official Trustee holds the proceeds for the wife and children.

t: Under the IRDAI Master Circular on Life Insurance (2024), a death claim that does not require any investigation must be settled within:
o: 90 days from date of intimation
15 days from receipt of all necessary documents
30 days from receipt of all necessary documents
45 days from receipt of all necessary documents
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). The timeline is 15 days where no investigation is required and 45 days where investigation is warranted; interest is payable for delay beyond these limits.

t: A policyholder nominates his wife and two sons without specifying their shares. On his death the policy money is:
o: paid wholly to the wife
paid wholly to the elder son
withheld until the nominees agree on shares
paid to the nominees in equal shares
e: Where several nominees are named without shares, insurers pay them jointly or in equal shares; the policyholder can avoid disputes by stating the percentage share of each nominee.

t: Letters of administration under the Indian Succession Act, 1925 are granted by the court where:
o: the deceased died intestate or without appointing an executor
the deceased left a will naming an executor
the policy carries a nomination
the sum assured is below ₹1 lakh
e: Probate is granted to an executor named in a will; letters of administration are issued to an administrator where there is no will or no executor, enabling him to collect the estate including policy money.

t: If the outstanding loan on a policy together with accrued interest exceeds its surrender value, the insurer may:
o: cancel the nomination
foreclose the policy after giving notice to the policyholder
recover the shortfall from the nominee
continue the policy without any action
e: Policy loans are secured only by the surrender value; once the debt exceeds it the security is exhausted and the insurer may foreclose, paying any balance to the policyholder.

t: The surrender value payable under a non-linked policy is:
o: always equal to the premiums paid
the guaranteed surrender value only
the higher of the guaranteed surrender value and the special surrender value
the paid-up value plus accrued interest
e: Guaranteed surrender value is the statutory minimum; insurers also compute a special surrender value based on the paid-up value, and the policyholder receives whichever is higher.

t: A policyholder whose policy lapsed six years ago, after it had acquired surrender value, approaches the insurer for revival. The insurer:
o: must revive it on payment of arrears with interest
must refund all premiums with interest
can revive it only with IRDAI permission
cannot revive the policy as the five-year revival period has expired, but the paid-up or surrender value remains available
e: Revival is possible only within the revival period (five years under the 2024 product regulations); thereafter the policyholder is left with the paid-up value or can surrender for the surrender value.

t: A unit-linked policy issued in March 2022 carries an annual premium of ₹3,00,000. On maturity, the proceeds will be:
o: exempt because the policy was issued before 2023
fully exempt under Section 10(10D)
taxable, as the annual premium exceeds ₹2,50,000
taxable only to the extent of 10% of the premium
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). For ULIPs issued on or after 1 February 2021 with aggregate annual premium above ₹2.5 lakh, the exemption under S.10(10D) is withdrawn and gains are taxed as capital gains; death benefit remains exempt.

t: For an early death claim, in addition to the death certificate, the insurer usually calls for:
o: the claimant's statement, hospital treatment certificate and employer's certificate of leave
a succession certificate only
a certificate from the agent only
the policyholder's income-tax returns for five years
e: These documents help verify the cause and circumstances of death and whether any illness pre-dated the proposal, which is relevant under Section 45.

t: A life assured dies while working in the Gulf. For proof of death, the insurer would normally accept:
o: a newspaper report of the death
a statement from the employer abroad alone
the death certificate issued by the foreign authority, duly attested by the Indian Embassy or Consulate
only a certificate issued by an Indian municipality
e: Foreign death certificates are accepted after attestation by the Indian mission, with translation where needed; the body's repatriation papers may also be examined.

t: On death, a policy carries sum assured of ₹8,00,000 and vested bonus of ₹1,20,000. A policy loan of ₹2,00,000 with accrued interest of ₹20,000 is outstanding. The amount payable to the nominee is:
e: Claim = 8,00,000 + 1,20,000 − (2,00,000 + 20,000) = ₹7,00,000; the outstanding loan and interest are deducted from the claim proceeds.

t: For a policy issued on or after 1 April 2013 on the life of a person with disability under Section 80U or a specified disease under Section 80DDB, the premium deductible under Section 80C is limited to:
o: 15% of the actual capital sum assured
10% of the actual capital sum assured
25% of the actual capital sum assured
20% of the actual capital sum assured
e: A higher limit of 15% applies to such persons, against 10% for other policies issued after 1 April 2012; the same thresholds govern exemption under Section 10(10D).

t: A policy that does not qualify under Section 10(10D) matures for ₹6,00,000, the total premiums paid being ₹4,50,000. Under Section 194DA (rate 2%) the tax deducted at source is:
e: TDS is on the income component only: (6,00,000 − 4,50,000) × 2% = ₹3,000, since the aggregate payout is ₹1 lakh or more.

t: The annuity received by an individual from a pension plan of an insurer is:
o: exempt up to ₹1.5 lakh per year
fully exempt under Section 10(10D)
taxable as income in the year of receipt
taxable only if it exceeds ₹5 lakh per year
e: While contributions attract deduction under S.80CCC, the pension received is taxable; only the commuted portion enjoys exemption under S.10(10A) to the prescribed extent.

t: The minimum capital required for registration as a direct insurance broker is:
o: ₹5 crore
₹4 crore
₹1 crore
₹75 lakh
e: Direct brokers need ₹75 lakh, reinsurance brokers ₹4 crore and composite brokers ₹5 crore under the broker regulations.

t: Third-party insurance is compulsory for a motor vehicle used in a public place under which section of the Motor Vehicles Act 1988?
o: Section 140
Section 146
Section 163A
Section 166
e: ★ Core fact (asked across III papers). Section 146 makes TP cover compulsory; Section 164 fixes no-fault compensation (₹5 lakh death / ₹2.5 lakh grievous hurt).

t: Under the IRDAI (Payment of Commission) Regulations, 2023, commission payable to agents and intermediaries is:
o: governed by the insurer's board-approved policy within the overall limits on expenses of management
fixed by the Life Insurance Council
prohibited on renewal premiums
capped at 35% of first-year premium for every product by regulation
e: The 2023 regulations removed product-wise commission caps and linked commission to the insurer's expenses-of-management limits, with a board-approved policy.

t: An agent of one life insurer wishes to also solicit business for another life insurer. Under IRDAI regulations he:
o: may do so if his annual premium income exceeds ₹10 lakh
must first surrender his existing agency, since an agent cannot represent two life insurers
may do so after informing both insurers
may do so with IRDAI's permission
e: An individual can hold only one life, one general, one health and one each of mono-line agencies; a second life agency requires surrender of the first, with a no-objection certificate.

t: Under the Indian Trusts Act, 1882, a trustee who holds a life policy in trust:
o: becomes the absolute owner of the policy
must be a bank or financial institution
holds it for the benefit of the beneficiaries and must deal with it according to the trust
cannot give a discharge for the policy money
e: Trustees hold legal title but are bound to apply the proceeds for the beneficiaries; MWP Act policies and group gratuity trusts are common examples in life insurance.

t: An 'alien enemy' (a citizen of a country at war with India) is:
o: competent to contract only through an agent
treated like any other foreigner
competent to contract if above 18 years
disqualified from contracting with an Indian insurer during the war, unless permitted by the Government
e: Section 11 excludes persons disqualified by any law; an alien enemy cannot enter into or enforce contracts in India while the hostilities continue, and existing contracts are suspended.

t: On nationalisation in 1956, the Life Insurance Corporation of India took over the life business of how many Indian and foreign insurers and provident societies in all?
e: LIC absorbed 245 entities: 154 Indian insurers, 16 foreign insurers and 75 provident societies; 107 is the number of general insurers nationalised in 1972.

t: By the General Insurance Business (Nationalisation) Amendment Act, 2002, the four subsidiaries of GIC were:
o: privatised and sold to foreign insurers
delinked from GIC, which became the Indian reinsurer
transferred to LIC
merged into a single company
e: National, New India, Oriental and United India became independent companies owned by the Government, and GIC Re was designated the national reinsurer.

t: The Right to Information Act, 2005 applies to the Life Insurance Corporation of India and IRDAI because they are:
o: listed companies
consumer organisations
public authorities established or controlled by the Government
members of the Life Insurance Council
e: Bodies constituted under a statute or substantially financed by Government are public authorities under S.2(h); policyholders use RTI to obtain information such as the status of their claims.

t: The Insurance Ombudsman scheme is administered by the:
o: Insurance Institute of India
Life Insurance Council
Central Consumer Protection Authority
Council for Insurance Ombudsmen (formerly the Executive Council of Insurers)
e: The Council for Insurance Ombudsmen, constituted under the 2017 Rules, appoints Ombudsmen, provides infrastructure and reviews their functioning.

t: A dispute over a repudiated life claim valued at ₹2.5 crore under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 lies before the:
o: National Commission
State Commission
District Commission
Insurance Ombudsman
e: The National Commission has original jurisdiction where the value of consideration exceeds ₹2 crore under the 2021 rules.

t: The Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) established under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 has the power to:
o: adjudicate individual consumer complaints against insurers
investigate unfair trade practices and misleading advertisements and order recalls or refunds, including through class action
regulate insurance premium rates
appoint Insurance Ombudsmen
e: The CCPA is a regulator protecting consumers as a class, distinct from the three-tier commissions that decide individual complaints.

t: Since 1 April 2021, the standard fire policy for a dwelling in India is:
o: Standard Fire and Special Perils Policy
Bharat Griha Raksha
Bharat Sookshma Udyam Suraksha
Householder's Package Policy
e: ★ Core fact (asked across III papers). Bharat Griha Raksha for homes; Bharat Sookshma Udyam Suraksha (up to ₹5 crore) and Bharat Laghu Udyam Suraksha (₹5–50 crore) for enterprises.

t: Under Section 2(7A) of the Insurance Act, 1938, an 'Indian insurance company' is a company:
o: registered with the Reserve Bank of India
having at least 100 branches in India
formed and registered under the Companies Act, in which the aggregate foreign holding does not exceed the prescribed limit, carrying on only life, general, health or reinsurance business
wholly owned by the Central Government
e: The definition limits foreign shareholding (now 74%) and restricts the company to insurance business; only such a company can obtain registration under Section 3.

t: Section 14 of the Insurance Act, 1938 requires every insurer to maintain:
o: a register of shareholders only
a register of IRDAI circulars
a register of agents' deposits
a register of policies and a register of claims
e: The register of policies records the name of the policyholder, date, sum assured and any assignment or nomination; the register of claims records intimations, settlements and reasons for rejection.

t: Which of the following statements about the history of insurance legislation in India is INCORRECT?
o: The Insurance Act, 1938 established the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority
The Insurance Act, 1938 created the office of the Controller of Insurance
The Indian Insurance Companies Act, 1928 enabled collection of statistical information on insurers
The Life Assurance Companies Act, 1912 was the first legislation to regulate life insurance in India
e: The 1938 Act set up the Controller of Insurance; IRDAI was created only by the IRDA Act, 1999 following the Malhotra Committee's recommendations.

topic: Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority Act, 1999
t: Under Section 18 of the IRDA Act, 1999, the Authority is bound by:
o: resolutions of the Life Insurance Council
directions on questions of policy issued in writing by the Central Government
recommendations of the Insurance Advisory Committee
orders of the Insurance Ombudsman
e: The Authority must follow written directions of the Central Government on policy matters, after being given an opportunity to express its views; the Government's decision on what is a question of policy is final.

topic: Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority Act, 1999
t: Regulations made by IRDAI under Section 26 of the IRDA Act, 1999 must be:
o: ratified by the State legislatures
published only on the IRDAI website
made in consultation with the Insurance Advisory Committee and laid before each House of Parliament
approved by the Supreme Court
e: Section 26 requires consultation with the Advisory Committee and Section 27 requires the rules and regulations to be laid before Parliament, which may modify or annul them.
